questions.q: How does a rolling update differ from blue-green deployment, per this lesson?
options: It replaces a running service's instances gradually, inside the same environment, instead of standing up a second full environment
It requires exactly double the compute, just like blue-green
It can only be used for stateless services with no load balancer
It deploys the new version to every instance simultaneously
questions.explain: Rolling updates swap instances a few at a time in place, with no second full environment -- unlike blue-green's two parallel environments.

questions.q: What does 'max unavailable' control during a rolling update?
options: How many extra instances can exist temporarily above the normal count
How many instances are allowed to be down at once during the rollout
The total number of instances the service will ever have
How long the rollout is allowed to take, in minutes
questions.explain: Max unavailable caps how much capacity can drop during the rollout -- setting it to 0 means capacity never drops.

questions.q: What does setting max unavailable to 0 and max surge small produce, according to this lesson?
options: A rollout that finishes instantly with no side-by-side window
A rollout identical in cost and speed to blue-green
A rollout that skips verification entirely
A rollout that is slower, but capacity never drops and extra cost stays small
questions.explain: That's the conservative configuration the lesson describes: slow, but safe, with capacity never dropping.

questions.q: Why can a rolling update briefly serve two different, both 'correct,' answers to the same question?
options: Because the load balancer is broken during a rollout
Because old and new instances run different, unrelated application code
Because old and new versions serve traffic at the same time, and can be running different model checkpoints
Because rolling updates always disable the model entirely during rollout
questions.explain: The side-by-side window means a request can land on an old-checkpoint instance or a new-checkpoint instance at the same moment, mid-rollout.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why can this side-by-side behavior matter more for a chat-style AI app than a one-off completion?
options: Because chat apps never use load balancers
Because a session that hits a different instance each turn mid-rollout can feel like the assistant changed its mind, even though it's just load balancing
Because chat apps are always deployed with blue-green instead of rolling updates
Because rolling updates are not compatible with chat-style applications
questions.explain: The lesson's example: inconsistency across turns in a session reads as the model behaving oddly, when it's actually two checkpoints both being live during the rollout.
